speaker: guide
text: Welcome. Enter your name, then your matriculation number.

speaker: narrator
text: Abuja. A dispute over the Federation Account has reached the Supreme Court.

speaker: narrator
text: In seventy-two hours, the Federal Government and the states meet to ask how such disputes should be settled.

speaker: narrator
text: Spain is the model on the table. Seventeen regions. Different powers. Different fiscal deals. Yet the conflict has never fully gone away.

speaker: narrator
text: You are the analyst. What can Nigeria borrow from Spain, and where does the comparison break?

speaker: eze
text: I need a brief I can defend at the retreat. We will compare Spain with Nigeria, then decide what travels and what does not.

speaker: guide
text: What is your starting position on Spain? Choose the view closest to your own.

speaker: eze
text: Then show me how. Start with Catalonia.

speaker: eze
text: Then show me where it breaks.

speaker: eze
text: Then show me why.

speaker: guide
text: You have twenty-four research hours. Open at least two sources. Each new source costs six hours. Save time if you want to check your recommendations later.

speaker: guide
text: Catalonia is already open. This first source costs you no research hours.

speaker: marin
text: No single model. Seventeen autonomous communities. Powers devolved region by region, at different speeds. The centre keeps wide powers to coordinate.

speaker: marin
text: The Basque Country and Navarre have a special fiscal regime. They collect most taxes and pay the State a negotiated sum for State services.
trigger: Open or replay Basque Country & Navarre

speaker: marin
text: The statute was reformed in 2006. The Constitutional Court limited parts of it in 2010. The 2017 referendum was ruled unlawful, and Article 155 was invoked.

speaker: marin
text: Andalusia is in the common regime. It is funded through a national formula and transfers. Disputes centre on how fair the formula is.

speaker: guide
text: Choose the claim your reading can support. Then attach two of the sources you opened.

speaker: guide
text: Asymmetry breeds tension because each region measures fairness against another’s deal.

speaker: guide
text: The open constitutional design leaves fiscal terms permanently renegotiable.

speaker: guide
text: Tension is driven by nationalist party mobilisation.

speaker: guide
text: Litigation has replaced political bargaining.

speaker: eze
text: The evidence carries the claim.

speaker: eze
text: Half of this is assertion. The retreat will find it.

speaker: eze
text: Nothing here supports that.

speaker: guide
text: Three disputes are arriving. Choose the institution that should handle each one. Your decision locks when you confirm it, and earlier choices can make the next dispute harder.

speaker: eze
text: Madrid and the Basque government disagree on the annual payment under their fiscal agreement.

speaker: eze
text: Several regions say the common funding formula shortchanges them.

speaker: eze
text: A regional parliament passes a law the central government says exceeds regional powers.

speaker: eze
text: A regional parliament passes a law the central government says exceeds regional powers. The region now says it will ignore an adverse ruling.

speaker: guide
text: Which mechanism fits this dispute?

text: Settled in the bilateral commission. No court needed.

speaker: marin
text: The council handles the common formula, not the Basque payment.

speaker: marin
text: Slow and adversarial. The agreement has its own commission.

speaker: marin
text: Last resort. Spain used it in 2017, after the Court, not before.

speaker: sani
text: One region’s deal fuels others’ grievance.

speaker: eze
text: Talks open with all regions. No ruling, no winner. The centre keeps the final say.

speaker: marin
text: The Court judges legality, not funding formulas. The politics stays unresolved.

speaker: marin
text: Last resort. Spain used it in 2017, after the Court, not before.

speaker: marin
text: A private deal over a public law does not settle the constitutional question.

speaker: marin
text: The council cannot rule on legality. The law stays in force.

speaker: eze
text: The government challenges. The law is suspended. The Court must confirm or lift this within five months.

speaker: marin
text: Last resort. Spain used it in 2017, after the Court, not before.

speaker: eze
text: The Court rules against the region. The region does not comply. You now have a further decision.

speaker: eze
text: The law stays in force, and the region keeps its position.

speaker: eze
text: A quiet settlement, in the most asymmetric case. Does that fit your thesis?

speaker: guide
text: Invoke Article 155 now, or let the Court use its own enforcement powers first?

speaker: marin
text: Intervention needs an absolute Senate majority. Order is restored faster, but regional grievance deepens.

speaker: marin
text: Since 2015, the Court can enforce its rulings, including fines and suspension of officials. Slower enforcement keeps the centre’s legitimacy while tension persists.

speaker: eze
text: Three Spanish features. Tell us what Nigeria can take, and what it cannot.

speaker: marin
text: Spain’s system works because of how it was built, not only what it contains. Copy the parts and you may miss that.

speaker: sani
text: Spain has no resource control history. We do. Start there.
trigger: Roundtable opening 3; subject expert review before release

speaker: guide
text: For each feature, choose Transfer, Adapt, or Reject. A source check costs six reserve hours. You can decide without a check, but borrowing without checking raises fit risk.

speaker: guide
text: Bilateral fiscal deals for particular regions.

speaker: sani
text: Give one state a special deal and thirty-five will want theirs.

speaker: marin
text: The Basque and Navarre arrangements rest on historic rights recognised in the Constitution itself. They were not designed as a template.

speaker: guide
text: Sector conferences and signed cooperation agreements.

speaker: sani
text: Spain’s calm owes something to shared parties. Ours do not always align.

speaker: marin
text: Sector conferences, cooperation agreements and party alignment each help prevent contestation.

speaker: guide
text: Automatic suspension of a contested regional law while the Constitutional Court decides.

speaker: sani
text: Our Supreme Court already hears these cases. And this power would sit in Abuja.

speaker: marin
text: The power sits in Spain’s Constitution, Article 161.2, and lapses after five months unless the Court confirms it. Nigeria would need an amendment.

speaker: sani
text: You have reopened resource control.

speaker: marin
text: Keep the principle: open, rules-based arrangements any state can qualify for.

speaker: eze
text: Safe. But you lose Spain’s lesson on transparent, negotiated rules.

speaker: eze
text: No amendment needed. Do it.

speaker: marin
text: Reasonable, but do not overbuild what already works.

speaker: marin
text: Then states keep reaching for the courts first.

speaker: sani
text: Abuja could freeze any state law. No.

speaker: eze
text: With what safeguard? Otherwise it is a weapon.

speaker: marin
text: In Spain the centre holds it. Your states would never accept that.

speaker: marin
text: Rejecting is easy. What would you borrow?

speaker: sani
text: You have just shown us what Abuja would do with it.
trigger: Borrow Card C after Article 155 follow-up

speaker: guide
text: There are not enough reserve hours for another check. The earlier sources remain in your brief notes.

speaker: guide
text: Close your brief with one usable lesson and one Nigerian limit. Choose a lesson, then the limit that qualifies it.

speaker: guide
text: Nigeria can use regular sector conferences and written cooperation agreements to resolve disagreements before litigation.

speaker: guide
text: Nigeria can adapt transparent negotiated fiscal rules so that every state has a fair route to participation.

speaker: guide
text: Nigeria can match each dispute to negotiation, coordination or adjudication before choosing a response.

speaker: guide
text: Nigeria can learn from Spain by seeking better outcomes and keeping an open mind about reform.

speaker: guide
text: But the constitution and the equal status of states constrain how such arrangements can be introduced.

speaker: guide
text: But party alignment and state-centre trust will shape whether cooperation works in practice.

speaker: guide
text: But resource control, derivation and FAAC politics limit the case for copying special fiscal deals.

speaker: guide
text: But progress will depend on everyone making a strong effort and remaining positive about change.

speaker: eze
text: That goes in the brief.

text: The retreat has begun. A delegate will test the weakest part of your brief. Your earlier choices are on the table.
